items.readable_text:
Content:
One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

Content:
As an example, we consider the [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: [1|− 2; 0|− 1]] with the diagonalization
[MATH: [5|1; 0|1]]

Content:
We will use the diagonalization of [MATH: A] to compute [MATH: A^{55}.]

Content:
Let's start by computing [MATH: A^2.] Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have

Content:
[MATH: A^{2}|= PDP^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = PDP^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = P(DD)P^{− 1}; = PD^{2}P^{− 1}.]

Content:
Computing [MATH: A^3,] we get

Content:
[MATH: A^{3}|= A^{2} ⋅ A; = PD^{2}P^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = PD^{2}P^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = P(D^{2}D)P^{− 1}; = PD^{3}P^{− 1}.]

Content:
We see that the matrix [MATH: P] and its inverse [MATH: P^{-1}] will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that

Content:
[MATH: A^{\color{blue}55}=P \cdot D^{\color{blue}55} \cdot P^{-1}.]

Content:
Now, we only need to find [MATH: D^{\color{blue}55}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:
[MATH: D^{2}|= [1|0; 0|− 1][1|0; 0|− 1] = [1^{2}|0; 0|(− 1)^{2}]; D^{3}|= D^{2}D = [1^{2}|0; 0|(− 1)^{2}][1|0; 0|− 1] = [1^{3}|0; 0|(− 1)^{3}]]

Content:
Following this pattern, we get

Content:
[MATH: [1^{55}|0; 0|(− 1)^{55}]]

Content:
Therefore, we can conclude that
[MATH: A^{55}|= [5|1; 0|1][1|0; 0|− 1]^{55}[(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [5|1; 0|1][1|0; 0|− 1][(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [5|− 1; 0|− 1][(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [1|− 2; 0|− 1].]

Content:
In general, given that [MATH: A = PDP^{-1},] for any non-negative integer [MATH: {\color{blue}k},] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: A^{\color{blue}k} = P \cdot D^{\color{blue}k} \cdot P^{-1}.]

This idea also works in reverse. Given a diagonalization [MATH: A] in the form

[MATH: A=PDP^{-1},]

Content:
we can immediately deduce that the eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are the diagonal entries of [MATH: D,] and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of [MATH: P.] This is because the diagonalization of a matrix is (almost) unique.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Raising a Diagonalizable Matrix to a Power

Content:
One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

Content:
As an example, we consider the [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix [MATH: [1|− 2; 0|− 1]] with the diagonalization
[MATH: [5|1; 0|1]]

Content:
We will use the diagonalization of [MATH: A] to compute [MATH: A^{55}.]

Content:
Let's start by computing [MATH: A^2.] Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have

Content:
[MATH: A^{2}|= PDP^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = PDP^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = P(DD)P^{− 1}; = PD^{2}P^{− 1}.]

Content:
Computing [MATH: A^3,] we get

Content:
[MATH: A^{3}|= A^{2} ⋅ A; = PD^{2}P^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = PD^{2}P^{− 1} ⋅ PDP^{− 1}; = P(D^{2}D)P^{− 1}; = PD^{3}P^{− 1}.]

Content:
We see that the matrix [MATH: P] and its inverse [MATH: P^{-1}] will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that

Content:
[MATH: A^{\color{blue}55}=P \cdot D^{\color{blue}55} \cdot P^{-1}.]

Content:
Now, we only need to find [MATH: D^{\color{blue}55}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:
[MATH: D^{2}|= [1|0; 0|− 1][1|0; 0|− 1] = [1^{2}|0; 0|(− 1)^{2}]; D^{3}|= D^{2}D = [1^{2}|0; 0|(− 1)^{2}][1|0; 0|− 1] = [1^{3}|0; 0|(− 1)^{3}]]

Content:
Following this pattern, we get

Content:
[MATH: [1^{55}|0; 0|(− 1)^{55}]]

Content:
Therefore, we can conclude that
[MATH: A^{55}|= [5|1; 0|1][1|0; 0|− 1]^{55}[(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [5|1; 0|1][1|0; 0|− 1][(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [5|− 1; 0|− 1][(1)/(5)|− (1)/(5); 0|1]; = [1|− 2; 0|− 1].]

Content:
In general, given that [MATH: A = PDP^{-1},] for any non-negative integer [MATH: {\color{blue}k},] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: A^{\color{blue}k} = P \cdot D^{\color{blue}k} \cdot P^{-1}.]

[MATH: [3|6; 1|1]]

Therefore, [MATH: E] is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of [MATH: E] are [MATH: \lambda_1=3] and [MATH: \lambda_2=6] and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix [MATH: P.] Computing [MATH: P,] we obtain
[MATH: P = [3|6; 1|1]^{− 1} = (1)/(− 3)[1|− 6; − 1|3] = [− (1)/(3)|2; (1)/(3)|− 1].]
In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are

[MATH: [− (1)/(3); (1)/(3)]]
